outcome: No proof or disproof of pi's normality has appeared since 26 January 2024; all activity in the window is computational digit-record extension (120+ trillion, then 314 trillion digits) and statistical/empirical studies consistent with (but not establishing) normality, plus one unrelated general theoretical paper on normal numbers that does not mention pi.
summary: The question of whether pi is normal (every digit and digit-string equally frequent in some/every base) remains completely open, exactly as it was on 26 January 2024, and I found nothing that changes what a careful person would write in this bullet. Within the window: (1) record-setting digit computations continued — over 120 trillion digits in early 2025 and 314 trillion digits by late 2025 (Razeto & Rossi, arXiv:2608.06438, 'Can π generate itself? A Monte Carlo analysis of 314 trillion digits'), which I opened and confirm is a Monte Carlo / statistical-randomness study using pi's digits as a pseudorandom source, explicitly not a proof of normality — it only extends empirical consistency to more digits, which per §3.1 does not advance an existence/'is it normal' question. (2) A 2025 MDPI paper (Mathematics 13(2):313) claims to bound the probability of normality via a Bernoulli-experiment hypothesis test on the first 100 million digits ('1.86×10^30 times more likely that π is normal than not') — this is probabilistic/statistical argument, not a mathematical proof, and the source itself (per search snippets, since the page returned HTTP 403 and could not be opened directly) frames it as evidence rather than resolution; I was unable to fetch the full text to confirm AI involvement, but nothing in the abstract-level description suggests AI. (3) 'Super-Dense Sets and Their Role in the Theory of Normal Numbers' (arXiv:2506.15422, opened) is a general topological theory paper about normal vs. non-normal numbers as a class; it never mentions pi and does not bear on this specific constant — a related-but-different question under §3.1, so it does not count as a case or progress on pi's normality. (4) A blog post/informal piece ('Pi vs. AI: Could a Neural Network Predict the Next Digit of Pi?') describes a neural network failing to predict pi's digits beyond ~10% (chance) accuracy — this is an informal, non-peer-reviewed exploration that, if anything, is weak empirical evidence consistent with randomness/normality, not a proof, and not indexed as a mathematical contribution; I did not find any peer-reviewed or expert-digested account crediting an AI system with mathematical progress on this problem. The Wikipedia 'Pi' article, current as of this check, still states plainly that 'The conjecture that π is normal has not been proven or disproven,' with no updated claim of progress. No source anywhere in my search claims a case of normality (e.g., a specific base, or a specific finite digit-string frequency bound proven exactly) was settled, nor any bound that would count as 'progress' under §6.1 in a way that changes the open status. I am satisfied this is a genuine 'nothing happened' record rather than an under-searched one.
competing_reading: One could argue the 314-trillion-digit Monte Carlo paper and the 100-million-digit Bernoulli hypothesis-test paper constitute 'progress' in a loose sense (extending empirical/statistical support), but per §3.1 an infinitude/universal-property question like normality is not advanced by more computation or a probabilistic likelihood argument — only an actual proof or disproof (or a rigorously proven partial/restricted case, e.g. proven normality in one specific base) would count. Neither exists in the window, so I classify as open/no_change_found rather than progress.
what_would_settle_it: A rigorous proof (or disproof) that pi is normal in some base, or a peer-reviewed proof of a genuine restricted case (e.g., normality of pi in a specific base, or a proven non-trivial digit-frequency bound derived from provably-established structure rather than statistical testing), would change this record's status to partial or resolved.
